title: Glide check-up
name: typing_glide_checkup_title
description: Measure your own swipes, get one change proposed with its expected effect, and confirm it later
help: Two of the numbers behind glide typing depend on what you write rather than on the keyboard: how much of the dictionary a swipe may answer with, and how much a word's commonness counts against the shape you drew. The check-up finds the right values from your own swipes. While it is measuring, each word you swipe is read again in the background under a few candidate values, and only the words that come out are kept, never the stroke. After 30 swipes it proposes one change at a time, says how many of your own swipes it would have read right, and lets you apply it. After the next 40 swipes it compares how often you corrected swiped words before and after, and offers to keep or undo. A change is never applied or undone over a value you set by hand in the meantime.

title: Emoji categories
name: langemoji_emoji_categories_title
description: Reorder the tabs, hide the ones you never open, and arrange the emoji inside each
help: The emoji panel ships its categories in Unicode's own order, which is rarely the order you reach for them in. Drag a category to move its tab, and press the eye to hide a tab you never open. Press a category to arrange the emoji inside it: press and hold one, then drag it where you want it. The Recent tab and the Kaomoji tab are not listed here. Recent orders itself by use, and the Kaomoji tab has a page of its own, Kaomoji, on the Emoji panel page.

title: Arrange like
name: langemoji_emoji_order_preset_title
description: Put the tabs and the emoji in the order of Gboard, SwiftKey or HeliBoard
help: Pick the keyboard you used before, and the emoji panel gets its tabs, in its order, with each emoji where that keyboard puts it. The grid also changes to that keyboard's columns, row height and emoji size, so the same swipe scrolls to the same emoji. Some keyboards keep plants with the animals and the weather with travel and places. Those emoji then move to that tab, and a tab with nothing left in it is hidden. An emoji that keyboard does not have yet goes next to the emoji it follows. After you pick one, you can still drag tabs and emoji. Unicode puts everything back the way it shipped.

title: Added emoji
name: langemoji_emoji_added_title
description: Add emoji that are newer than the keyboard, one at a time or from Unicode's emoji-test.txt
help: Each Unicode release adds new emoji. Until an update of WM Keyboard includes them, you can add them here. An added emoji shows at the end of its tab in the emoji panel. You can search for it by its name and keywords, make it a favourite, and it shows in Recent. When an update includes the emoji, its row here says so and you can delete it. Added emoji go into your backups and sync with your settings.

title: Download automatically
name: customdict_emoji_auto_download_title
description: Download keywords for the languages that you type
help: When you turn a language on, the app downloads its emoji keywords in the background. This is about 100 KB, one time. If you turn this off, the Download buttons below are the only way to get the keywords.

title: Shift and Enter type a new line
name: typing_shift_enter_title
description: Add a line break in a chat app instead of sending the message
help:
Chat and search fields tell the keyboard that Enter means Send, Go or Search. Usually you cannot put a line break in a message without sending it. With this setting on, press shift first, or hold shift on a physical keyboard, and Enter types a real new line. The Enter key shows the new line symbol while shift is armed, so you can see the result before you press it.

Shift stays armed for as long as you leave it up, so a message can run to as many lines as you like. It comes back down when you type a letter or press shift again.

You can also hold shift down while you tap Enter.

In a document app such as Google Docs or Word, which has no Send of its own, shift and Enter reach the app as a real Shift+Enter. Those apps start a new line inside the paragraph for it and a new paragraph for Enter alone.

Only a shift that you press yourself counts. The keyboard ignores the shift that automatic capital letters arms at the start of a message, so the first line of a message still sends. The keyboard also ignores caps lock.

Turn it off to follow the Enter action of the app whatever shift is doing.

title: Volume keys move the cursor
name: typing_volume_cursor_title
description: Volume up and volume down move the text cursor
help: While the keyboard is open, volume down moves the cursor one character left, and volume up moves it one character right. Press and hold a key to repeat. Everywhere else, and as soon as the keyboard closes, the volume keys work as usual.

title: Release the keys while audio plays
name: typing_volume_cursor_media_title
description: Keep the volume control while something plays
help:
While music, a video or a podcast plays, the volume keys change the volume again, even with the keyboard open. You can always turn the sound down while you type a reply. Cursor control comes back when the audio stops.

Turn this off to make the volume keys always move the cursor while the keyboard shows.

title: Autocorrect
name: typing_autocorrect_title
description: Fix typos automatically when you press space
help: When you press space, the keyboard compares the word you typed with the word list. If the word looks like a slip of a much more common word, the keyboard replaces it. The keyboard never corrects a word that you taught it. Autocorrect stays off in password fields. To turn it off for one language only, open that language in Languages & layouts.

title: Autocorrect confidence
name: typing_autocorrect_confidence_title
description: How certain the keyboard must be before it corrects a word
help: The keyboard corrects a word only when the best candidate scores higher than the second candidate by this factor. A low value corrects more typos, but it guesses wrong more often. A high value corrects only when the word is almost certain. The keyboard always applies a correction that two sources agree on.

title: Adaptive confidence
name: typing_autocorrect_adaptive_title
description: Correct less eagerly when you undo corrections often
help: The keyboard tracks how often you undo its corrections. When you undo corrections often, the keyboard raises the confidence it needs before it corrects a word. When you rarely undo corrections, the confidence returns to the value of the slider. The keyboard also remembers each correction you undo, one word pair at a time. "Remember my undos" sets how long that memory lasts.

title: Typing rhythm
name: typing_timing_signal_title
description: Let your typing speed sway autocorrect
help: The keyboard measures how fast you type each word. When you type in a fast burst, typos are likely, so autocorrect fires more eagerly. When you type slowly and deliberately, for an unusual name or a word from another language, autocorrect holds back. The slider sets how strongly the rhythm sways the decision. Zero turns the signal off.

title: Adapt to app tone
name: typing_register_priors_title
description: Casual words rank higher in chats, lower in email
help: Chat words such as "lol" and "gonna" rank a little higher in messaging apps, and a little lower in email apps and email fields. This only reorders the suggestions. No word is ever hidden or blocked, and autocorrect does not change.

title: Undo autocorrect with backspace
name: typing_undo_autocorrect_title
description: Backspace right after a correction restores what you typed
help: Press backspace immediately after autocorrect changes a word. The keyboard puts your original spelling back and learns it, so it does not correct that word again. Turn this off to make backspace always delete one character.

title: Undo a correction from the strip
name: typing_undo_chip_title
description: Show a chip that puts back the word you typed
help: Backspace undoes a correction only in the moment. Type one more letter and the correction is out of reach, and this is when you usually see it. With this on, the keyboard puts a chip at the start of the suggestion strip with your own spelling on it. Press the chip and the keyboard puts that word back, and learns not to make the same correction again. The chip appears between words and stands until you end the sentence. Not every correction gets one. The setting below says which corrections do.

title: How often to offer the undo
name: typing_undo_chip_obviousness_title
description: A higher setting puts the chip on more corrections
help: Most corrections need no undo. The keyboard was sure, the change was small, and you can see what happened. A chip after every one of those is clutter, and you learn to look past it. This setting sets the bar. The keyboard scores each correction on two things. The first is how sure the keyboard was. The second is how far the new word is from what you typed. A short word with one neighbouring letter changed scores high. A guess, or a word split in two, scores low. A correction that scores under this bar gets a chip. At the lowest setting almost no correction does. At the highest setting every correction does.

title: Remember my undos
name: typing_undo_memory_title
description: How long a correction you undo stays undone
help: When you undo a correction, the keyboard remembers that exact pair of words and stops making the same correction. This setting says how long the keyboard keeps that memory. The keyboard reads an undo in two ways. Backspace, pressed right after the correction, is a clear undo. The keyboard also checks the text later, and counts it as an undo when your own spelling stands where the correction was. The second reading is weaker. You can go back to fix a typo by hand without seeing that the keyboard already fixed it, and type the same typo again. On every level except Strict, the keyboard ignores that second reading when your spelling is not a word it knows.

title: Stop after I refuse a fix
name: typing_stop_after_declines_title
description: Leave a word alone once you have undone or deleted its correction this many times
help: Sometimes autocorrect changes a word, you delete the change and type your word again, and autocorrect changes it again. This setting ends that loop. Each time you undo a correction or delete it, the keyboard counts one refusal for that word in that place. When the count reaches this number, the word you type there stays as you typed it, and the keyboard does not offer the fix on the strip either. Only that one place in that one text field is affected. The same typo anywhere else is still corrected, and the count is gone when you leave the field. Never turns this off.

title: Learned correction gate
name: typing_learned_gate_title
description: Judge each fix by everything the keyboard knows about it
help: Autocorrect used to apply a fix when the best candidate beat the runner-up by a fixed factor. The learned gate weighs everything at once: how far ahead the candidate is, what kind of slip explains the typo, how long the word is, whether your own words agree with the word list, what the context model thinks, and how fast you typed. It was fitted on thousands of typed sentences and on new words typed correctly, so it holds back from rewriting names and slang more often. The Autocorrect confidence slider moves its bar the same way. Off uses the fixed factor as before.

title: Learn from my fixes
name: typing_learn_corrections_title
description: Typos you fix by hand teach autocorrect
help: When you go back and fix a word by hand, the keyboard remembers what you typed and what you changed it to. Fix the same typo twice and autocorrect makes that fix for you from then on. After one fix it offers the fix on the strip instead. The keyboard also learns the slip behind each fix, such as hitting 3 for e or b for the space bar, so the same slip in other words is understood. Undo a learned fix and the keyboard stops making it. A word that is itself a real word, like form for from, only changes after three fixes and when the words around it agree.

title: Learn where my taps land
name: typing_adapt_taps_title
description: Words you keep teach the keyboard how you miss each key when tapping
help: Nobody taps the exact middle of every key. With this on, every word you type and leave standing records where your finger landed on each letter, and later taps are read against keys moved to match. A slip toward a neighbouring key is then corrected the way you actually make it. Swipes have their own version of this under Glide typing. Turn it off to freeze what has been learned, or use Forget below to start over.

title: Mistype tolerance
name: typing_mistype_tolerance_title
description: How far into a neighbouring key a tap may land and still count as a slip
help: Every tap is read against where it landed, not only against the key it hit, so a tap near the edge of a key can still be read as the key next to it. This sets how generous that reading is. Above 100%, a tap well inside a neighbouring key is still a likely slip, which suits fast or hectic typing and big fingers. Below 100%, the key you hit is trusted more, which suits careful typing. It changes which words the strip offers and what autocorrect picks. The default is 100%.

title: Fix several missed keys
name: typing_fix_several_slips_title
description: Correct a word even when more than one tap landed a little off its key
help: Every tap is read against where it landed, so a tap near the edge of a key can count as the key next door. This reads every letter of a word that way at once, so a word typed quickly with three or four keys a little wide still comes out right. Careful only suggests a fix that also needs a letter added or removed, because that mix is what most often turns a correctly typed new word, name or slang into some other word. Eager applies those fixes too, which suits a dictionary that already holds every word you type. A word the keyboard knows is never changed, and one you keep typing is learned after a few uses.

title: Skip words in capital letters
name: typing_skip_all_caps_title
description: Leave words typed in capital letters alone
help: You usually type acronyms, or words in capital letters for emphasis, on purpose. Examples: ASAP, OFC, NOOO. Autocorrect leaves every word in capital letters alone. Turn this off to correct these words like any other word.

title: Correct the word before Enter
name: typing_autocorrect_on_enter_title
description: Enter corrects the last word, as space does
help: Enter ends a word the same way space does, so autocorrect can change the word before it. In a search box or a chat, Enter also sends the text, and you cannot see the correction before it goes. Turn this off to send the last word as you typed it. Space still corrects words.

title: Correct the word before punctuation
name: typing_autocorrect_on_punctuation_title
description: A full stop, comma, ! or ? corrects the last word, as space does
help: With this on, a mark that ends a word corrects it the same way space does: "teh!" becomes "the!". The marks are . , ! ? ; : and the Bengali danda (।). A slash, a bracket or a symbol does not count. With this off, a word ended by a mark goes in exactly as typed, which is safer when you type abbreviations or names the word list does not know. One backspace right after the mark puts the word back as you typed it.

title: Capitals from the word list
name: typing_dictionary_capitals_title
description: Write a word with the capital letter that its word list gives it
help: Some word lists spell words with a capital letter, such as the nouns in German and the names of places. When you type or swipe one of these words in small letters, the keyboard writes it with its capital letter. A word that the list also spells in small letters stays as you typed it. Backspace immediately after the word puts back what you typed. This uses the word list that you downloaded for the language. For the built-in English list, the keyboard carries the capitals of days, months, places, names, acronyms and the word I itself.

title: Block offensive words
name: typing_block_offensive_title
description: Keep profanity and slurs out of the suggestions
help: The keyboard does not offer offensive words in the suggestion strip. Autocorrect does not change a neutral typo into an offensive word. You can still type any word yourself. This setting only stops the suggestions.

title: Context-aware suggestions
name: typing_context_rerank_title
description: Reorder suggestions by the words around them
help: The keyboard reorders the top suggestions with the words you typed before them: your own word pairs, common English pairs, and words from the current conversation. The reorder applies only when there is real evidence, so the usual order stays for unfamiliar contexts. This never changes which word autocorrect applies.

title: Context model
name: typing_neural_context_title
description: Read the whole sentence to predict and rank words
help: A small language model, downloaded for your language, reads the sentence you have typed so far and says which words are likely to come next. It fills the next-word suggestions, helps order corrections, and backs the learned autocorrect gate. It runs on this device and needs no network once downloaded. A word it does not know, such as a name or a word you taught the keyboard, is left to your dictionary as before. Turning this off reads no model file.

title: Re-check the previous word
name: typing_context_revision_title
description: Offer a fix for the word before, once the next word shows what you meant
help: After you type a word, the keyboard looks again at the word before it with the new word in sight. If one of the other readings it had fits the sentence much better ("by a car" → "buy"), a chip offers it. Nothing changes until you tap the chip. Needs the context model.

title: Phrase suggestions
name: typing_phrase_completion_title
description: Offer the next few words as one chip
help: After a space, the strip can offer two or three words at once, when the context model is sure of each of them. Tap the chip to type them all. Needs the context model.

title: Add missing spaces
name: typing_autocorrect_splits_title
description: Split two words typed together when you press space
help: When the word you typed is unknown, but it divides into two words the keyboard knows, the keyboard can commit the two words with a space between them: "ofthe" becomes "of the". It does this only for a pair the keyboard has seen together, in the language's word pairs or twice in your own typing, and never for a word in your personal dictionary, so a name or term the word list lacks is not cut in two. A letter next to the spacebar can also stand in for the space itself, so "amibtomake" becomes "ami tomake", when that tap landed low on its key, toward the spacebar. The split applies only when no single word explains the typed text. Otherwise it stays a suggestion on the strip. Backspace right after the split puts your text back, like any other correction. With this setting off, the suggestion strip stops offering two-word splits as well.

title: Remember each app's language
name: typing_language_detection_by_app_title
description: Start from the language you usually write in this app
help: The keyboard keeps a tally, per app, of which of your languages the words you type there belong to. When you open a text field in that app, detection starts from that tally instead of from nothing, so a new message in a chat app you write Banglish in leans Banglish before you have typed a word, and a new email starts out English. The lean is worth about one typed word of evidence at most, so the first word you actually type outweighs it and a message in the other language is never fought. Apps with only a few dozen words of history lean less. The tally stays on this device and is wiped with the rest of the learned data.

title: Detect the language you type
name: typing_language_detection_title
description: Follow the language of the current message
help: When your languages share a keyboard, the words already in the text field show which language you write now. The keyboard leans its suggestions and autocorrect toward that language, and swings back when you switch. Type "ami tomake" on the English keyboard and it behaves like the Banglish one; type "how are you" and it behaves like English again. This works per text field and needs languages with "Also suggest from" set up, which romanized languages get automatically.

title: Detection strength
name: typing_language_detection_strength_title
help: Gentle only reorders suggestions and never lets the detected language win over the keyboard's own. Balanced lets a clearly detected language take the lead, and autocorrect follows for all but the most common words. Aggressive hands over completely, so autocorrect fixes typos in the detected language even against very common words of the keyboard's own language.

title: Fix number row slips
name: typing_number_row_corrections_title
description: Correct a stray digit to the letter below it
help: With the number row on, a tap meant for the top letter row can land on a digit, and "as3" appears instead of "ase". With this setting on, one digit inside a word can be corrected to the letter below it when you press space. The correction only ever swaps the digit for a letter. A word that starts with a digit, and a word with two or more digits, never change. This setting has an effect only while the number row is shown.

title: Fix missing apostrophes
name: typing_auto_apostrophe_title
description: arent → aren't, im → I'm, dont → don't
help: You type a contraction without its apostrophe (arent, isnt, youre, oclock…). When you press space, the keyboard puts the apostrophe back, and a lone "i" becomes "I". The keyboard leaves alone the words that are also real English words without the apostrophe (its, well, ill, shell…). This setting works even when autocorrect is off.

title: Automatic capital letters
name: typing_auto_capitalize_title
description: Put a capital letter at the start of each sentence
help: Shift turns on by itself at the start of a text field, and after the punctuation that ends a sentence (. ! ? ।). This happens only in the fields that ask for sentence capitals, and only in the scripts that have capital letters, which are Latin, Cyrillic, Greek and Armenian. Nothing changes in Bengali or any other script without letter case. The keyboard never changes caps lock by itself.

title: Shift changes the case of the selection
name: typing_shift_recase_title
description: Shift with text selected steps through lowercase, Title Case and UPPERCASE
help: When you select text and press shift, the keyboard changes the case of the selection. It does not arm shift for the next letter. Each press steps through lowercase, Title Case and UPPERCASE. Nothing changes for the scripts without case, such as Bengali. Turn this off to keep shift for the next character only, even while text is selected.

title: Shift changes the case of the word before the cursor
name: typing_shift_recase_caret_title
description: With nothing selected, shift changes the word that ends at the cursor
help:
Put the cursor right after a word and press shift. The word steps through lowercase, Title Case and UPPERCASE, and the cursor stays where it is. The shift key follows the word: Title Case puts shift on, and UPPERCASE is caps lock. This works as on SwiftKey.

A word that only starts at the cursor does not change. While you type a word, shift is still for the next letter. When the cursor touches no word, shift works as usual.

title: Shift changes the case of the word around the cursor
name: typing_shift_recase_inside_title
description: With nothing selected, shift changes the word the cursor is inside
help:
Put the cursor inside a word, as in "cur|sor", and press shift. The whole word steps through lowercase, Title Case and UPPERCASE, the same as for the word before the cursor.

Turn this off to keep shift for a capital letter in the middle of a word.

title: Double space
name: typing_double_space_title
description: What two quick presses of space type
help: Press space two times quickly at the end of a word. Full stop replaces the first space with a full stop, so you can end a sentence with no change to the symbols layout. Tab replaces it with a tab character, which helps with indents and forms. Two spaces leaves both spaces as they are.

title: Double space speed
name: typing_double_space_window_title
description: How quickly the two spaces have to follow each other
help: Two spaces closer together than this count as a double space and become a full stop or a tab. Raise it if you type slowly and never get the full stop. Lower it if you get full stops you did not mean. This setting is 400 ms by default.

title: Automatic space after punctuation
name: typing_auto_space_punctuation_title
description: The keyboard adds a space after you type . , ? ! ; or :
help: You do not need to press space at the end of a clause: "hello," becomes "hello, " by itself. A group of marks ("...", "?!") stays together. A mark typed straight after a number gets no space, so "5,000", "3.14" and "5:00" stay whole. A domain ending or file extension typed after a full stop closes back up, so "google. com" becomes "google.com". If you press space yourself, the keyboard does not add a second space. Shift immediately after the space removes it. The keyboard leaves structured fields alone: passwords, email addresses, web addresses, number pads and phone pads. A space in these fields is a mistake.

title: Remove a space before punctuation
name: typing_hug_punctuation_title
description: "Hey ." becomes "Hey." when you type the mark
help: A space typed by mistake in front of a punctuation mark is removed when the mark lands. The mark must come after a word, a number or a closing bracket, so a mark at the start of a line is left alone. One backspace right after puts the space back. Languages that put a space in front of a mark on purpose, French among them, are handled by the setting below and are never hugged, whichever marks are listed here. The keyboard leaves structured fields alone: passwords, email addresses, web addresses, number pads and phone pads.

title: Marks that pull the space out
name: typing_hug_punctuation_marks_title
description: One character for each mark, with no spaces between them

title: Space before French punctuation
name: typing_language_punctuation_spacing_title
description: "Bonjour!" becomes "Bonjour !" in French and its neighbours
help: French keeps a space in front of the exclamation mark, the question mark, the semicolon, the colon and the closing guillemet, and one behind the opening guillemet, and so do Breton, Occitan, Walloon, Picard, Norman and Franco-Provençal. The keyboard types that space for you and stops every other rule from taking it back. It is a no-break space, so the mark can never wrap to the next line on its own. The mark must follow a word, a number or a closing bracket, so one at the start of a line is left alone. One backspace right after removes the space again. Every other language types exactly as before. The keyboard leaves structured fields alone: passwords, email addresses, web addresses, number pads and phone pads.

title: Space after a suggestion
name: typing_space_after_suggestion_title
description: Add a space when you select a word from the suggestion strip
help: This setting is on by default. When you press a suggestion, the keyboard types the word and a space after it, so the next word starts clean. Turn it off to type the word without the space. This helps in the languages or fields where a space after a word is usually wrong. If you go back to a word and continue it, the keyboard never adds a second space. To turn it off for one language only, open that language in Languages & layouts.

title: Wrap the selection with brackets
name: typing_wrap_selection_title
description: Press either half of ( ) [ ] { } < > " ' or ` to put the pair around the selected text
help: When you select text and press a bracket, a brace or a quote key, the keyboard puts the pair around the selection. It does not replace the selection. Either half of the pair works. Example: select "foo", press ( or ) and you get "(foo)". The wrapped text stays selected, so you can wrap it again. Turn this off to make these keys always replace the selection, like any other character.

title: Close brackets for me
name: typing_auto_close_brackets_title
description: Press ( [ { and the keyboard types the closing half, with the cursor between them
help: This setting is off by default. With it on, pressing an opening bracket types the closing one behind the cursor and leaves the cursor between the two, so you type straight inside the pair: press ( and you get (), ready for what goes in it. Pressing the closing bracket when it is already the next character steps over it instead of typing a second one, and one backspace on an empty pair takes both halves out. The CJK brackets are included, and so are the fullwidth ones. Quotes are not: the apostrophe in "don't" shares that key, and closing it would be wrong more often than right. Nor is <, which outside code is a less-than sign. Passwords, email fields and number pads are left alone; a browser's address bar is not.

title: Continue lists
name: typing_continue_lists_title
description: Enter after "1. milk" types "2. " on the next line, in any app
help: This setting is off by default. With it on, pressing Enter on a line that starts with a list marker starts the next line with the next one: - * + and • carry on as they are, 1. and 1) count up, and a task box such as - [x] or ☐ carries on as an empty box. The indentation in front of the marker is kept. Pressing Enter on an item with nothing after its marker ends the list: the marker is taken off and no new line is typed. A number has to be three digits or fewer, so a line that opens with a year is left alone. Only fields where Enter makes a new line take part; a chat box that sends on Enter sends as usual, and Shift+Enter there makes the list line. Passwords, email fields, web addresses and number pads are left alone.

title: Suggestions
name: typing_suggestions_title
description: Show word predictions above the keyboard
help: The keyboard shows up to three candidates above the keys while you type: completions, corrections and next word predictions. The keyboard learns the predictions from your typing. Press a candidate to type it with a space after it.

title: Number of suggestions
name: typing_suggestion_slots_title
description: How many words the suggestion strip shows at once
help: The strip splits its width evenly between the suggestions, so more of them means each one is narrower and long words are shrunk further to fit. Three suits a phone. A tablet or a landscape screen has room for more. This setting is 3 by default.

title: More slots for short words
name: typing_fit_more_words_title
description: Show up to three more suggestions when they are short enough to fit without shrinking
help: The strip still starts from Number of suggestions. When the next words are short, it adds slots for them, up to three more, as long as every word fits its share of the strip at full size. Long words keep the usual number of slots. It does nothing while the suggestions scroll or are kept in place. This setting is off by default.

title: Swipe down for more suggestions
name: typing_suggestion_pages_title
description: Swipe down on the suggestions to see every word the keyboard ranked
help: The strip shows only a few words. With this on, swipe down on it while it has words and a grid of up to 24 suggestions covers the keys, best first. Tap one to use it, or swipe the strip again or tap Back to the keys to close the grid. When this is on, a downward swipe over suggestions opens the grid instead of hiding the keyboard; over an empty strip it still hides it if that setting is on. This setting is off by default.

title: Emoji in the grid
name: typing_suggestion_pages_emoji_title
description: After the words, the emoji that match the word you are typing

title: Fancy text in the grid
name: typing_suggestion_pages_fancy_title
description: Last, the word in every fancy text style, to pick by how it looks

title: Swipe up for more suggestions
name: typing_suggestion_swipe_up_title
description: Swipe up on the suggestions, then slide onto a word and lift to use it
help: With this on, swipe up on the strip while it has words and up to 12 more suggestions open just above it. Keep your finger down and slide it onto the word you want: lift there to use it, or lift anywhere outside the words to close them without picking. This setting is off by default.

title: More suggestions in a grid
name: typing_suggestion_expanded_grid_title
description: Line the extra suggestions up in columns, one for each suggestion slot

title: Emoji takes a slot
name: typing_suggestion_emoji_slot_title
description: Count a suggested emoji as one of the suggestions
help: Suggested emoji normally ride after the words, up to four of them, on top of the number of suggestions. With this setting on, the best emoji takes the last slot and the words get one fewer, so the strip never shows more than the number of suggestions. Emoji suggestions are turned on and off under Emoji. This setting is off by default.

title: Suggested emoji
name: typing_suggestion_emoji_count_title
description: How many emoji ride after the words
help: How many suggested emoji can follow the words on the strip, from one to four. Four is the default. While an emoji takes a slot, the slot holds one, whatever this says. Emoji suggestions are turned on and off under Emoji.

title: Keep suggestions in place
name: typing_suggestion_fixed_slots_title
description: Same-width slots, and the best word never moves
help: Normally the words share the strip between them: two words split it in half, and an emoji, a row of punctuation marks or a tool's chip pushes the words aside to make room. With this setting on, the strip is always cut into the number of suggestions, every slot the same width, and a slot with nothing to show stays empty. The best word keeps the slot it always has. Anything that is not a word takes a slot of its own: a suggested emoji or the punctuation marks the last slot, a tool's keyword chip the first. This setting is off by default.

title: Coloured suggestions
name: typing_suggestion_tinted_title
description: Put each word on a pill of the theme's accent colour
help: Each suggestion sits on a rounded pill in the theme's accent colour, with the best word's pill the deepest, so the slots are told apart by colour rather than by thin dividers. With a Material You theme the colour follows your wallpaper. This setting is off by default.

title: Scroll the suggestions
name: typing_suggestion_scroll_title
description: Show each word at full size, and every word found, in a strip that scrolls sideways
help: Normally the strip splits its width evenly and shrinks long words to fit their slot. With this on, every word keeps its natural size and the strip scrolls sideways instead. The strip also carries on past the number of suggestions, through every word the keyboard found, so the one you want is a swipe away even when it ranked fourth or tenth. Short words still fill the visible part as before. Turn it on if you want five or six suggestions on a narrow phone, or if your word is often not among the first few. This setting is off by default.

title: More suggestions arrow
name: typing_suggestion_more_arrow_title
description: An arrow at the end of the strip that opens every word found
help: When the strip scrolls and the keyboard found more words than fit, an arrow at its right end opens all of them in a grid. Turn this off to give that space back to the words. A swipe down on the strip still opens the same grid. This setting is off by default.

title: Punctuation suggestions
name: typing_punctuation_suggestions_title
description: Chips for . , ? ! and ' beside the word candidates
help: The keyboard adds a short row of common punctuation to the end of the suggestion strip while candidates show. A full stop or a comma is one press away, with no change to the symbols layout. A press acts the same as the key. When the keyboard offers an emoji prediction, the emoji takes the end of the strip instead.

title: Suggestions in every field
name: typing_suggestions_all_fields_title
description: Show the suggestion strip even where an app asks to hide it
help: Some apps, such as Instagram and Google Keep, tell the keyboard to hide the suggestion strip on ordinary text fields. This setting is on by default, and the keyboard shows the strip anyway, as most keyboards do. Turn it off to follow the app and hide the strip. In the address bar of a browser it also lets the keyboard complete the words that you type, though it never autocorrects them there. Autocorrect, glide typing and Bengali (Avro) composing work either way, because they no longer depend on the strip. Password fields and number pads never show suggestions.

title: Learn a word after
name: typing_learn_threshold_title
description: How many times you type a word before autocorrect leaves it alone
help: The keyboard never corrects a word it has learned from you. That protects your names and slang, but it also means one typo you commit once is protected forever. Raise this to make the keyboard wait until it has seen the word more than once. Suggestions are not affected: a word below this count can still be offered, it is just not shielded from correction. This setting is once by default.

title: Remember a new word after
name: typing_new_word_sightings_title
description: How many times you type a word nothing recognises before it is saved
help: Only words that no dictionary knows are counted. A word already in a dictionary needs one use, not several, because there is nothing in doubt about its spelling. Either way a use only counts once you have moved on and left the word alone, so a word you go back and fix, or a swipe that came out as the wrong word, is never counted. Nothing is saved while you are still typing: the words you left alone are added when you close the keyboard, send the message, or move to another field. Lower this if your own names and slang take too long to stick. Set it to 1 to save every new word after a single use. This setting is 3 by default.

title: Ask before saving new words
name: typing_ask_before_learning_title
description: Offer a chip instead of counting how often you type the word
help: When a word no dictionary knows is typed, the suggestion strip asks whether to add it. Tap the chip to save the word, or the ✕ to never be asked about it again. Nothing is saved unless you tap. Off by default, because a chip after a word you never think about again gets in the way.

title: Offer corrections it isn't sure about
name: typing_offer_near_miss_title
description: Show a chip for a fix that was close, instead of dropping it
help: Autocorrect has to be nearly certain before it changes a word on its own, because getting that wrong rewrites what you wrote and you may not notice. Everything just short of certain used to be thrown away, even when it was probably right. With this on, those appear as a chip at the start of the suggestion strip. Tap it to apply the fix, or carry on typing and it goes away. A correction you have already undone once is never offered. On by default, and it only ever appears where nothing used to happen at all.

title: Suggestion strip always visible
name: typing_suggestions_first_title
description: Keep the suggestion strip visible before you type
help: Usually the top bar shows the toolbar, and it changes to suggestions only while candidates exist. With this setting on, the top bar shows the suggestion strip at rest, so next word predictions are always visible. The arrow on its left opens the toolbar when you need a tool. With it off, an empty field shows only the toolbar, and its first word predictions are skipped.

title: Best suggestion in the middle
name: typing_primary_center_title
description: Show the best candidate in the middle slot
help: The best candidate, the one that autocorrect selects, goes in the middle of the strip. The second candidate goes on its left. Most keyboards use this layout. Turn this off to order the candidates from left to right.

title: Shorten long words
name: typing_suggestion_overflow_title
description: Where to cut a word that does not fit its slot
help: First, a long word gets smaller to fit its slot. If it is still too long, the keyboard removes some letters and shows an ellipsis (…) in their place. In the middle keeps the start and the end of the word, for example "Punct…tion". Most keyboards do this. At the end keeps only the start, for example "Punctuat…". This setting has no effect while Scroll the suggestions is on, because each word then keeps its full size.

title: Suggest contact names
name: typing_contact_names_title
description: Complete names from your contacts as you type
help: The words in your contact names complete in the same way as the words in the word list. Example: "was" gives Wasi. The names also chain: after Wasi, the keyboard offers the family name. The keyboard reads the names into memory only. It stores nothing and sends nothing, and autocorrect never changes a name that it knows. This setting needs the Contacts permission.

title: Suggest contact emails
name: typing_contact_emails_title
description: Complete the email address of a contact as you type it
help: Type the start of the email address of a contact, for example "john". The keyboard offers the full address (john.doe@gmail.com) in the suggestion strip. The keyboard reads the addresses into memory only. It stores nothing and sends nothing, and autocorrect never changes them. This setting needs the Contacts permission.

title: Contact emails in email fields too
name: typing_contact_emails_in_email_fields_title
description: Show them even where the app hides the suggestions
help: Email fields usually tell the keyboard to hide the suggestion strip. This would hide these completions where they help most. With this setting on, contact email completions still show in email fields. Other suggestions stay hidden there. Turn it off to follow the field, and complete email addresses only in ordinary text.

title: Remember email addresses you type
name: typing_typed_emails_title
description: Offer them in the next email field
help: When you type an email address into a field that asks for an email address, the keyboard keeps it. The next time an email field opens, the addresses you used most show on the suggestion strip before you type, and typing the start of one narrows the list. It learns only from email fields, never from ordinary text. The addresses stay on this phone. To delete them, use Storage in the settings.

title: Remember numbers you type
name: typing_typed_numbers_title
description: Type the first digits of one again and the strip offers the rest
help: When you type a number of three digits or more on its own and then press space or enter, or leave the field, the keyboard keeps it. The next time you type its first digits, the numbers you typed most that start with them show on the suggestion strip, and one tap types the rest. Digits stuck to letters, like win10, and the parts of a number split by a comma, a colon or a dash, like 1,234 or 12:30, are left alone. Nothing is kept from password fields, in incognito, or while Learn from typing is off. Number and phone fields have no suggestion strip, so this works in ordinary text fields. The numbers stay on this phone. To delete them, use Storage in the settings.

title: Suggest app names
name: typing_app_names_title
description: Complete the names of installed apps as you type
help: The words in the names of your installed apps complete in the same way as the words in the word list. Example: "sign" gives Signal. Autocorrect never changes one. They rank below contact names, because ordinary words such as Files and Clock are also app names. The keyboard reads the names into memory only. It stores nothing and sends nothing, and it needs no permission.

title: Inline emoji search
name: typing_inline_emoji_search_title
description: Type ":" and a word to find emoji, such as :smi for 😄
help: Type a colon at the start of a word to change the suggestion strip into an emoji search. ":cat" offers 🐱, and a press replaces the text you typed. Press backspace over the colon to go back to normal word suggestions. Press space to keep the text exactly as you typed it.

title: Password manager suggestions
name: typing_inline_autofill_title
description: Show saved logins from your autofill service in the suggestion strip
help: When you select a login field, your password manager can offer saved entries as chips in the suggestion strip, instead of a separate popup. The password manager draws the chips itself. The keyboard gets only their size, and never sees the user name or the password inside them. The chips stay available in incognito mode, because they record nothing. This setting needs Android 11 or newer, and a password manager set as your system autofill service.

title: Password manager button
name: typing_password_manager_chip_title
description: In a password field with no saved login on the strip

title: Smart replies
name: typing_smart_replies_title
description: Let the system offer replies to the message you answer
help: Android System Intelligence can read the conversation on the screen and offer short answers, such as "On my way!". The answers show as chips beside the word suggestions, up to three at a time. The system draws them, not the keyboard. They come over the same channel as the password manager chips, but they count and switch apart from them. You can have saved logins in the suggestion strip without the system reading your messages, or the opposite. Incognito mode turns this off by itself. This setting needs Android 11 or newer, and only some apps offer replies.

title: Autopilot
name: typing_group_autopilot_title
description: Wider keys for likely letters

title: Only offer new words
name: typing_skip_typed_word_title
description: Leave out the word you have already typed
help: The suggestion strip normally keeps one slot for the word exactly as you typed it, which is how you keep a spelling the dictionary does not know. Turn this on and that slot is given to another suggestion instead, so all three offer something new. The cost is that a word the keyboard does not recognise has one fewer way to survive a correction, and the strip no longer shows you which candidate is the literal thing you wrote.

title: Word as typed first
name: typing_typed_word_first_title
description: Show what you typed in the first slot, wherever it ranks. A space still writes the bold word

title: Recent words
name: typing_recent_word_bar_title
description: Your last three words in a row above the strip, each with what else it could be, so you can fix one after you have typed past it
help: The three words you wrote last sit in a row above the suggestion strip, the newest on the right, each followed by what else it could have been: what the strip offered as you wrote it, the other readings of its swipe, and the spelling it had before you changed it from here. Tap one and only that word changes, where it stands; the word you are typing and the cursor stay put. Only words you wrote in the field join the row. It is left out of password fields and incognito, starts empty in every new field, and shows in web address bars. Under Rows & bars you can move the row, put the words at the start of the strip instead, and keep the row's height while it is empty.

title: Numbers from the letter keys
name: typing_number_prediction_title
description: Type qwe with the number row off and the strip also offers 123
help: With the number row off, the top row of letters shows a small digit in each corner. When every letter of the word you are typing sits on one of those keys, the strip offers the number those digits spell in its last slot, beside the words, and one press types it. The word itself is never replaced without a press. Two or more letters are needed, so a single I or a single A stays a word. A number of five digits or more is grouped with separators when Group long numbers is on, using its grouping style. Nothing is offered while the number row is shown, since the digits are then on their own keys. This setting is off by default.

title: Words on the keys
name: typing_group_octopus_title
description: Next word over its key

title: Word menu
name: typing_word_menu_title
description: What pressing and holding a suggested word offers
help: Press and hold a word on the suggestion strip to open a menu about it. "Edit" is always there: it opens a card that spells, weights and ranks the word, shows where it comes from, and carries the Never suggest, Add and Delete actions, so you can turn those off to keep the menu short. "Add" only appears while you type a word that is not in your personal dictionary, and "Delete" only for a word the keyboard can forget. "Synonyms" lists words with the same meaning, and tapping one puts it in place of the word. It appears for English words.

title: Synonym sources
name: typing_synonym_sources_title
description: Where the word menu looks for synonyms, in order
help: The keyboard asks the first source that is on. When it has no synonyms for the word, or cannot be reached, the keyboard asks the next one. Drag a source to change the order, and turn off a source to never ask it. Online sources receive only the word you held, and a look-up is not stopped by Data saver, because you ask for it.

title: Adjust rank changes
name: typing_rank_control_title
description: What the word card's rank controls edit
help: Learned weight edits the same count the personal dictionary shows: how often the keyboard thinks you typed the word. It cannot push a word below a word list's own order, and 0 forgets the word. Rank adjustment keeps a separate up-or-down setting for the word that applies on top of every list, so any word can move either way without changing what the keyboard learned. Both by default, one control under the other.

title: Delete edits imported lists
name: typing_delete_edits_lists_title
description: Deleting a word takes it out of your imported word lists
help: Deleting a word from the suggestion strip forgets it from your personal dictionary, the waiting room, your rank adjustments and Android's dictionary. With this on, a word that is also in a word list you imported is removed from that list's file too, so it is gone for good; a word in a downloaded list, which cannot be edited, goes on the blacklist instead. With this off, imported lists are left as you imported them and the word is blacklisted the same way, so it stays hidden until you choose Suggest again.

title: Autopilot
name: typing_smart_hit_detection_title
description: Quietly widen the touch area of letters you are likely to type next
help: As you type a word, the word list predicts the letters that come next. The keyboard makes the touch area of each key larger toward those letters. A press that lands just inside the key next to it still gives the letter you wanted, but only near the shared edge. The keyboard never changes a press in the middle of a key. This works on the letters layer only, and it needs Suggestions on.

title: Strength
name: typing_autopilot_strength_title
description: How far a likely letter reaches over the key next to it
help: At 1 the keyboard changes a press only at the exact edge between two keys. At 10 a likely letter claims most of the space between itself and a letter that the word list does not expect. From 11 to 20 it pushes further still, until it reaches the limit. A letter never reaches more than about one key width away, whatever you set here. 5 is the value the keyboard started with.

title: Show the effect
name: typing_autopilot_show_title
description: Draw a favoured letter at the size its touch area has grown to
help: The keyboard draws each expected letter over the board at the size autopilot gave it, so you can see what Strength does while you type. The keys themselves do not move, and you press them in the same places. At most three letters are drawn at a time, and they are the three the word list expects most. The drawing shows only while you type. It goes away during a glide, and it does not come back when you move the cursor into a word.

title: Size of the effect
name: typing_autopilot_size_title
description: How much bigger than life a favoured letter is drawn
help: ×1.0 draws each touch area at its true size. A higher value multiplies the growth alone, so a letter that claimed no extra space stays the size of its key and only the difference gets larger. This changes the drawing and nothing else: your presses land in the same places at every value. The outline follows the same size, so the two always agree.

title: Outline the touch areas
name: typing_autopilot_outline_title
description: Draw the boundary each expected letter has claimed
help: A thin line marks the edge each expected letter has grown to. Use it to tune Strength. The line traces the same edge that Show the effect draws, so the two always agree. The line is a tuning aid, so turn it off again when you are done.

title: Animate the touch areas
name: typing_autopilot_animate_title
description: Ease the enlarged letters and outlines to their new size instead of jumping
help: With Show the effect or Outline the touch areas on, each expected letter normally jumps to its new size on every keystroke. Turn this on and the areas grow and shrink smoothly, and fade in and out as letters gain or lose favour. It only changes the drawing. The touch areas you type against change at once, as before. Reduce motion turns this off.

title: Change the system clipboard too
name: clipboard_copy_rules_system_title
description: So a paste from any app's own menu gets the tidied text
help: With this setting off, the rules change only what the clipboard history keeps, and what the keyboard pastes from it. Turn it on and a copy a rule changed is put back on the system clipboard as changed, so the paste menu of every app gets it too. A clip its app marked as a password is never changed. This setting is off by default.

title: Plain letters
name: clipboard_plain_letters_title
description: Keep copies in fancy fonts as the plain letters they stand for
help: Some apps and websites write in decorated letters: bold or italic letters from the math alphabets, script and double-struck letters, full-width letters, circled and squared letters, small capitals, and lines drawn through or under each letter. Copied, they paste the same way, and a search box or a screen reader cannot read them. With this setting on, the clipboard keeps the plain letters instead, before any rule runs. Symbols such as ™ and ℃ stay as they are. To tidy clips that are already in the history, select them in the clipboard and press Tidy. This setting is off by default.

title: Remove trackers from copied links
name: clipboard_clean_links_title
description: utm_source, fbclid and the like come off every link you copy, so every paste is clean
help: Each link in a copy loses the query parameters that only track where it was shared, the same ones the selection bar's Remove trackers takes off, and your own names below. Sites like Amazon, YouTube, X, TikTok and Google lose the trackers they add themselves, and a redirect link (Google's /url, Facebook's l.php, an Outlook safe link) becomes the link it leads to. The rest of the link, and the rest of the text, stays as it was. The clean link is put back on the system clipboard, so the paste menu of every app gets it too. Press Undo right after pasting it to get the link as you copied it. A clip its app marked as a password is never changed. This setting is off by default.

title: Words on the keys
name: typing_octopus_enabled_title
description: Float a predicted word over the key you would press next
help: The keyboard writes a small word above the key that would carry on the word you are typing. With "hel" typed, "hello" sits over the l, "help" over the p. Flick up on that key, or tap the word itself, and the whole word is written. After a space the keyboard offers whole next words above their first letters instead. The suggestion strip keeps working as before; this only adds to it. The BlackBerry Z10 typed this way, and it is what the Octopus keyboard copied.

title: Where the words sit
name: typing_octopus_placement_title
description: Above the key, in a lane of their own, or inside the key
help: Above the key puts each word in the gap over its key, half on the key and half above it, and the keyboard stays the same height. Own lane gives every row a strip of its own so nothing overlaps anything, and the keyboard grows a little taller. Inside the key writes the word over the letter, which never overlaps but leaves both very little room.

title: How many words
name: typing_octopus_density_title
description: How many words may sit on the keys at once
help: At 3 or 4 only the words the keyboard is confident about appear, which is how the BlackBerry did it, and the board often stays empty. Higher values fill more keys, and past 9 the keyboard looks up a word for every key it can, which is how the Octopus keyboard did it. The board never shows a word it cannot fit; a key too narrow for the word is left bare.

title: What may appear
name: typing_octopus_kinds_title
description: Which kinds of guess are allowed onto the keys
help: Completions carry on the word you are typing. Corrections fix it, and sit over the key where the word stops matching what you typed, so they are drawn in a different colour. Next words appear after a space, above their first letters, before you have typed anything. Turning all three off leaves the keys bare, the same as turning the whole feature off.

title: While gliding
name: typing_octopus_glide_title
description: What the keys carry while a swipe is being drawn
help: A stroke and a still finger want different things from the keys, so a glide has its own answer here and What may appear is left to say what a typed word may offer. Nothing keeps the board bare until you lift, which is what most glide typists want: mid-swipe a completion cannot be taken and a correction cannot be judged. Other readings floats the alternatives the keyboard is still holding, each above the key that reaches it, so you can steer to one. The next word offers what would follow the word you are drawing, above the key it starts with, so it can be flicked the moment the swipe ends. Whichever you choose, lifting your finger puts the next word on the keys as usual.

title: Flick up to pick
name: typing_octopus_flick_title
description: A quick upward flick off a key writes its word
help: Flick up from a key carrying a word and the whole word is written. What counts is the direction, not the speed: the stroke has to go up, and go there fairly straight. A stroke that leans or curves is treated as the start of a glide instead. A flick that misses simply types the letter. With words on the keys turned on, a glide that begins straight upward off a key that is carrying one is harder to start; that is the trade.

title: Flick sensitivity
name: typing_octopus_sensitivity_title
description: How far off straight up a flick may lean and still pick
help: Each setting is a cone around straight up, and how straight the stroke has to be. Strict asks for an unmistakably vertical, unmistakably straight flick, which is what you want if you glide a lot and find your swipes being taken as picks. Relaxed accepts almost anything upward, for boards where the words matter more than the swipes. Balanced sits between them.

title: Tap the word to pick
name: typing_octopus_tap_title
description: Tapping the small word itself writes it
help: Tap directly on a floating word to write it. This is easier to find than the flick, but the words are small targets. Words on the top row hang partly above the keyboard, and only the half over the key can be tapped; the flick works on all of them.

title: Word size
name: typing_octopus_size_title
description: How large the floating words are drawn
help: A multiple of the size the small corner hints use. Larger words are easier to read but overlap their neighbours sooner, and a word that no longer fits over its key is dropped rather than shortened past reading.

title: Hide the corner hint
name: typing_octopus_hints_title
description: A key carrying a word drops its long-press hint
help: The small character in a key's top corner and a floating word are close enough together to read as one thing. With this on, a key showing a word hides its corner hint for as long as the word is there; keys with nothing to say keep theirs.

title: Long-press characters too
name: typing_octopus_long_press_title
description: Allow words that need a long press to reach their next letter
help: Off by default. A word floating over a key promises that pressing that key writes the next part of it, and a character you can only reach by holding the key breaks that promise. Turning this on reaches more words, at the cost of some keys offering a word that a press alone will not finish. It changes nothing on an English QWERTY board, where the long-press characters are digits and accents that no English word uses: it is for a word like café or für on a board that keeps its accents behind a hold.

title: Words per key
name: typing_octopus_stack_title
description: How many words one key can carry, stacked
help: One word per key is what the BlackBerry and Octopus keyboards drew, and it is all a phone-sized key has room for. On a tablet the keys are tall enough for two or three, stacked away from the key with the likeliest word nearest it. A flick up takes the nearest word; a tap takes the word you touch. How many words still caps the whole keyboard.

title: Blocked from the keyboard
name: backup_blacklist_scope_title
description: Where a word you block with Never suggest applies
help: Pressing and holding a suggestion and choosing Never suggest blocks the word. This decides whether it is blocked in every language or only in the language you were typing. Words you add on this screen ask each time.

title: Smart chips
name: typing_smart_chips_title
description: Answer sums, conversions and tool keywords in the suggestion strip
help: When a tool can answer the text you typed, the suggestion strip offers the answer instead of word candidates. Press the answer to type the result. Press the button on its right to open the full tool with the same numbers in it. The keyboard recognises everything on your device. It downloads only exchange rates, and only after you type an amount in a currency.

title: Calculate as you type
name: typing_smart_calc_title
description: "12*4" offers 48

title: Convert currencies
name: typing_smart_currency_title
description: "150 usd", "150$" or "150 dollars" offers the amount in %1$s

title: Convert units
name: typing_smart_units_title
description: "1 ft" offers the same length in metres

title: Tool keywords
name: typing_smart_tool_keywords_title
description: Type "wiki" and the strip offers to open Wikipedia
help: Each tool has a few keywords. Type one keyword alone and the suggestion strip offers to open that tool and delete the word you typed. The settings of each tool list its keywords, where you can change them or clear them.

title: Resolve dates
name: typing_smart_dates_title
description: "next friday" offers the date it lands on, and the calendar opened there

title: Answer weather questions
name: typing_smart_weather_title
description: "will it rain" shows the forecast on the strip. Needs a weather location

title: Offer lookups
name: typing_smart_lookups_title
description: "define serendipity" offers the dictionary, "who is Tesla" offers Wikipedia

title: Translate hints
name: typing_smart_intents_title
description: "how do you say" or "in spanish" offers the translator

title: GIFs for celebrations
name: typing_smart_gifs_title
description: "happy birthday" offers a matching GIF search

title: Group long numbers
name: typing_smart_numbers_title
description: Type 1234567 and the strip offers it grouped. One press types the grouped number
help: A number of five digits or more, typed on its own, is offered back with separators. Numbers that start with a zero are left alone, and so is anything joined to a letter, a dash or a slash, because those are phone numbers, dates and codes rather than amounts.

title: Call or text a contact
name: typing_smart_contacts_title
description: Type the name of a contact and the strip offers to call or text that person
help: Type the full name of a contact, in any case, or only the first name with a capital letter when no other contact has that first name. The strip then shows a chip with the name. Tap the name to open your phone app with the number filled in. Tap the message button to open your messages app. The keyboard never makes the call itself, and the name that you typed stays in the text. Each name is offered one time in each text field. This setting needs access to your contacts and is off by default.

title: Repeated text
name: typing_smart_repeats_title
description: Type the same thing a few times in a row and the strip offers the Text repeat tool
help: Type a word, a phrase or a line and then type it again, with a space, a comma or a new line between, or with nothing between, such as "hahaha". Once it is there the set number of times, a chip shows the text with a count that goes up as you keep typing it. Tap the chip and the Text repeat tool opens on that text, with the same separator and a larger count ready. The text you typed stays until you press Insert there, and the tool's own setting says whether Insert replaces those copies or adds to them. Each text is offered one time in each text field. A single stretched letter or a doubled emoji does not count, and the chip does not show in password fields.

title: Chip after this many repeats
name: typing_smart_repeat_after_title
description: How many copies in a row before the chip shows

title: Keep the text when a chip opens its tool
name: typing_smart_keep_text_title
description: The settings button on a chip leaves what you typed, such as 150 usd or calculator, in the text
help: The button at the end of a chip opens the tool with your numbers filled in. When this is off, the button also removes the text that the chip answered, because the tool types its own result in its place. When this is on, your text stays. Either way, if the tool typed nothing, the first backspace after you close the tool puts the removed text back.

title: Grouping style
name: typing_smart_number_grouping_title
description: Where the separators fall

title: Codes from notifications
name: typing_otp_chip_title
description: When a verification code arrives in a notification, offer it above the keys. One press types it
help: The keyboard watches incoming notifications for a one-time code. When it finds one, a chip with the code and the name of the app that sent it appears above the keys. Press the chip to type the code. This needs notification access. The keyboard reads notifications on your device only, keeps the code in memory only, and sends nothing anywhere. Turn this off and the keyboard stops reading notifications at once.

title: Allow notification access
name: typing_otp_access_title
description: The chip cannot see codes arrive yet. Press to open the system switch

title: Only in code boxes
name: typing_otp_code_fields_title
description: Show the chip only where the app asks for a code, rather than in every field
help: A code box usually asks for a number keypad, or names itself "OTP", "PIN" or "verification code". With this on, the chip shows there and nowhere else. Some apps give their code box neither, and the chip cannot find it — leave this off and a code is offered in any field while it is still valid.

title: Offer a code for
name: typing_otp_expiry_title
description: A code older than this stops being offered

title: Clear the notification
name: typing_otp_dismiss_title
description: Dismiss the code's notification after the chip types it
help: A used code has no reason to stay in the shade. After the chip types the code, the keyboard dismisses the notification it came from. This uses the same notification access. Some apps post their code again after a dismissal; turn this off if that bothers you.

title: Your own code words
name: typing_otp_keywords_title
description: Words that come before a code in your messages, commas between. Example: 验证码, 口令

title: Type codes one character at a time
name: typing_otp_per_digit_title
description: For the forms that give each character of a code its own box
help: Many apps and websites split a code across a row of small boxes, one character each, and move to the next box for you. A whole code sent at once goes into the first box, which keeps one character and drops the rest. With this on, the keyboard types the code character by character, so each box gets its own. This applies to codes from notifications and to codes pasted from the clipboard.

title: Glide typing
name: typing_glide_typing_title
description: Swipe across the letters to type a word
help: Swipe your finger from letter to letter without a lift. The keyboard types the word when you lift your finger. Other readings show in the suggestion strip, so one press corrects a wrong guess. This works with every language when the layout has the letters to spell its common words. It stays off on a layout that converts what you type, such as the Chinese and Japanese ones.

title: What a swipe does
name: typing_letter_swipe_action_title
description: Glide a word, or pick a different use for a swipe across the keys
help:
Type words: a swipe across the keys spells one word. This is glide typing.

Handwrite: the keyboard reads a swipe across the keys as handwriting. Draw a letter or a word. After a short pause the keyboard recognises it and types it, and offers other readings in the suggestion strip. This needs a handwriting model (Settings → Handwriting). The F-Droid build doesn't have this option.

Slide to a key: put your finger down and slide it to the key you want. The keyboard lights the key under your finger and types only that key when you lift. The keys you slide across type nothing. Use this when your finger often lands on the wrong key. Lift outside the keys to type nothing. A drag from a key with flick directions, from the space bar or from the delete key keeps its own action.

With every option, a plain press still types its key.

title: Glide across the spacebar
name: typing_space_glide_multiword_title
description: Swipe over the spacebar to continue with the next word
help: Keep your finger down. Glide a word, swipe across the spacebar, then glide the next word. Each crossing types the word and a space, so one stroke gives a full phrase. When this setting is off, a swipe across the spacebar makes one word.

title: Two-thumb typing
name: typing_two_thumb_title
description: Tap and swipe with both thumbs at once to build one word
help: Use both thumbs together. Each thumb can tap or swipe, at the same time as the other, and every tap and swipe adds to the same word. For example, tap S with the left thumb, swipe O to M with the right, tap E with the left, then swipe T H I N G with the right, and you get "something". A tap that lands while the other thumb is still swiping goes into the word at that point, so a swipe over H E L O and a tap on L give "hello". Backspace removes the last tap or swipe from the word. Features that read one swipe as a whole word are off while this is on: the picker for a toss-up and its Hold to ask, gliding across the spacebar, and gliding over Shift for a capital.

title: Finish a two-thumb word
name: typing_two_thumb_word_end_title
description: What types the word you are building
help: With space, the word stays open while you tap and swipe, and the keyboard reads it again after each one. Tap space or punctuation to type it. With all thumbs up, the word is typed with a space once no thumb has touched the keyboard for a short pause, set below. A thumb that lands before the pause is over carries on the same word, so your thumbs can take turns. Tapped words end this way too.

title: Pause after a swiped word
name: typing_two_thumb_pause_title
description: How long both thumbs stay up before a word with a swipe in it is typed
help: With all thumbs up, a word is typed with its space only once no thumb has touched the keyboard for this long. A thumb that lands sooner adds to the same word, so your thumbs can take turns on one word without overlapping. This pause is for words with a swipe in them; words you only tap have their own below. Raise it if words end before you have finished them. Lower it if you wait too long for the space. The default is 350 ms.

title: Pause after a tapped word
name: typing_two_thumb_tap_pause_title
description: How long both thumbs stay up before a word you only tapped is typed
help: The same pause for words you only tap, so tapping T, lifting, and tapping O still gives "To". Taps leave longer gaps inside a word than swipes do, and stopping to think mid-word is normal when tapping, so you may want more time here than after a swipe. It starts at the swiped-word pause, 350 ms unless you changed that.

title: Pause after a one-letter word
name: typing_two_thumb_one_letter_pause_title
description: The least time a single letter waits before it is typed as a word
help: A single letter is far more often the start of a word than a word of its own, so it can wait longer than the pauses above. A word of one letter waits whichever is longer: this or its own pause. It starts at the shorter of the swiped-word and tapped-word pauses, 350 ms unless you changed them, which changes nothing until you raise it.

title: Take the space back
name: typing_two_thumb_retract_title
description: How soon after the space a letter can still carry the word on
help: If you stopped mid-word and the space came too early, carry straight on: a letter tapped or swiped within this time after the space takes it back and joins the word, as long as the two still lead to a word in the dictionary. Type car, let the space land, then pet, and you get "carpet". Type car, let the space land, then dog, and it stays "car dog". A letter after this time always starts a new word. It starts at twice the swiped-word pause, 700 ms unless you changed that. Slide it to the left end to turn it off.

title: Show the pause on the strip
name: typing_two_thumb_pause_band_title
description: A line under the suggestions shrinks until the word is typed
help: While your thumbs are up, a thin line along the bottom of the suggestion strip shrinks over the pause. When it is gone the word is typed with its space, and a thumb that lands before then takes the line away and carries on the word. With reduced motion on, the line stays whole until the pause is over.

title: Swipe finishes typed letters
name: typing_swipe_continues_typed_title
description: Typed letters and the swipe after them make one word
help: Type the start of a word, then swipe the rest without a space. For example, type T O and swipe G E T H E R to get "together". When this setting is off, the typed letters are a word of their own and the swipe types the next word. Two-thumb typing always works this way.

title: Glide over Shift to capitalize
name: typing_shift_glide_capitals_title
description: Draw through the Shift key mid-swipe for a capital letter
help: Gliding a name meant stopping to tap Shift first, which breaks the stroke. With this on, draw through the Shift key on your way and the word comes out capitalized; cross it twice and the whole word is in capitals. The key has to actually be crossed, and the walk out to it and back is cut from the path before the word is read, so the detour never adds a letter.

title: What a pass over Shift capitalizes
name: typing_shift_glide_mode_title
description: The whole word, or the letter you just left
help: Whole word: one pass capitalizes the word and a second pass makes it all capitals. One letter: each pass over Shift capitalizes the letter your finger came from, so a stroke can write HeLLo or LeanType, and ending the stroke on the Shift key makes the whole word capitals in one trip.

title: Ask when a glide is unclear
name: typing_glide_picker_title
description: Hold your finger still to choose between the closest words
help: Some swipes have no single right answer. On a fixed Bengali layout the letters ক and খ share a key, so a word and its aspirated twin are drawn exactly the same way, and on any layout a hurried swipe can fit two words equally well. When that happens, keep your finger down and hold it still for a moment: the closest words appear just above your fingertip. Slide onto one and lift to type it. Lift without choosing and the keyboard types its best guess, as it always did, and the same words stay on the suggestion bar either way. Once the words appear the swipe is finished, so sliding to a word does not change it. Slide down away from the words and lift to type nothing at all. The settings below decide how sure the keyboard has to be, how long to hold, and how many words to offer.

title: When to ask
name: typing_glide_picker_sensitivity_title
description: How close a call a swipe has to be before it asks
help: After a swipe the keyboard compares its two best readings. The closer they are, the less sure it is. Near ties asks only when the two words fit almost equally well. Close calls, the default, asks when the best word barely beats the next one. Any doubt asks whenever another word comes close. Every pause asks each time you hold still, whatever the keyboard thinks. The same words are on the suggestion bar either way.

title: Time to hold still
name: typing_glide_picker_dwell_title
description: How long to keep your finger still before the words appear
help: Hold your finger still for this long at the end of a swipe and the words appear. A short time answers faster but can open the words when you only paused to think in the middle of a word. A long time never opens them by accident but makes you wait. Small movements do not count: your finger can rest on the glass and drift a little.

title: Hold longer to always ask
name: typing_glide_picker_hold_title
description: A confident swipe still asks when you hold twice as long
help: When the keyboard is sure of a swipe it does not ask at the usual time. With this on, keep holding for twice the time and it asks anyway, so you can check any swipe before you lift. Turn it off and a swipe the keyboard is sure of never asks, however long you hold.

title: Words to choose from
name: typing_glide_picker_choices_title
description: How many words appear above your finger
help: Two to five words. Up to three fit in one row above your finger. Four or five use a second row above the first. More words give more choice, but each one is a smaller target to land on.

title: Learn my swipe style
name: typing_glide_swipe_style_title
description: Where your finger lands, how you draw each word, and which readings you correct
help: Nobody swipes through the exact middle of every key. A thumb cuts the far keys short and lands low on the near ones, and the keyboard used to charge every swipe for that.
